claim: The genus Drosophila provides roughly 1500 species including the model organism D. melanogaster.
source: Members of this genus, which provides roughly 1500 species including the model organism D. melanogaster, inhabit all continents except Antarctica, and occur in almost every type of environment.
evidence: This is stated as a factual assertion in the introduction without experimental data from this study, but is presented as established knowledge about the genus.

claim: Drosophila species inhabit all continents except Antarctica.
source: Members of this genus, which provides roughly 1500 species including the model organism D. melanogaster, inhabit all continents except Antarctica, and occur in almost every type of environment.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the geographic distribution of Drosophila.

claim: Closely related Drosophila species are known to utilize different types of food resources.
source: It is important to note that preferences in feeding and oviposition have shifted numerous times, and closely related species are known to utilize different types of food resources (Crowley-Gall et al., 2019; Crowley-Gall et al., 2016), or to visit a host at different stages of decay (Karageorgi et al., 2017; Keesey et al., 2015; Ometto et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Phylogenetically distant Drosophila species can use the same host or live in overlapping environments.
source: At the same time, it is common to find phylogenetically distant species using the same host, or living in overlapping environments (Hey and Houle, 1987; Lachance et al., 1995; Martin, 1998; Taylor, 1987; Taylor and Powell, 1978).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Members of the obscura species group overlap geographically and ecologically in their utilization of temperate forest ecosystems.
source: While little ecological information is available for a majority of the non-melanogaster species, it has been shown repeatedly that many of the members of the obscura species group overlap geographically as well as ecologically in their utilization of temperate forest ecosystems (Bächli et al., 2006; Burla et al., 1986; Michell and Epling, 1951).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Robust idiosyncrasies exist between visual and olfactory investment across the Drosophila genus.
source: In an earlier paper, we showed that robust idiosyncrasies exist between visual and olfactory investment across this genus (Keesey et al., 2019), including many examples of inverse variation within a subgroup, and between sympatric species and subspecies that utilize seemingly identical host plants or food resources.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: D. subobscura possessed much larger eyes in regards to surface area than D. pseudoobscura.
source: In general, we found that D. subobscura possessed much larger eyes in regards to surface area, as well as 25–30% more ommatidia than its close relative, D. pseudoobscura, though ommatidia diameter was identical (Figure 1A–E; Figure 1—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological measurements presented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 1.

claim: D. subobscura possessed 25-30% more ommatidia than D. pseudoobscura.
source: In general, we found that D. subobscura possessed much larger eyes in regards to surface area, as well as 25–30% more ommatidia than its close relative, D. pseudoobscura, though ommatidia diameter was identical (Figure 1A–E; Figure 1—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by ommatidia counts presented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Ommatidia diameter was identical between D. subobscura and D. pseudoobscura.
source: In general, we found that D. subobscura possessed much larger eyes in regards to surface area, as well as 25–30% more ommatidia than its close relative, D. pseudoobscura, though ommatidia diameter was identical (Figure 1A–E; Figure 1—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements of ommatidia diameter presented in the manuscript.

claim: D. subobscura exhibited larger dimensions in all measured body parts compared to D. pseudoobscura.
source: While there was some variation in individual size within and between species (with D. subobscura exhibiting larger dimensions in all measured body parts; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–E), we note that eye surface area was consistently correlated with ommatidium number (Figure 1D), suggesting that eye surface area provides a good approximation of visual investment.
evidence: This claim is supported by body size measurements presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Eye surface area was consistently correlated with ommatidium number in D. subobscura and D. pseudoobscura.
source: While there was some variation in individual size within and between species (with D. subobscura exhibiting larger dimensions in all measured body parts; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–E), we note that eye surface area was consistently correlated with ommatidium number (Figure 1D), suggesting that eye surface area provides a good approximation of visual investment.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Eye surface area provides a good approximation of visual investment in Drosophila.
source: While there was some variation in individual size within and between species (with D. subobscura exhibiting larger dimensions in all measured body parts; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–E), we note that eye surface area was consistently correlated with ommatidium number (Figure 1D), suggesting that eye surface area provides a good approximation of visual investment.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed correlation between eye surface area and ommatidium number.

claim: Both D. subobscura and D. pseudoobscura had a nearly identical linear relationship between surface area and number of ommatidia.
source: Here, we note that both of these two species had a nearly identical linear relationship between surface area and number of ommatidia (Figure 1D), with D. subobscura possessing larger eyes.
evidence: This claim is supported by the linear regression analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: D. pseudoobscura females displayed larger antennal surface areas relative to D. subobscura females.
source: While D. pseudoobscura possessed smaller eyes and a reduced ommatidium count, females of this species instead displayed larger antennal surface areas relative to D. subobscura females (Figure 1A–C,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by antennal surface area measurements shown in Figure 1.

claim: The maxillary palps did not display any significant variation in surface area between D. subobscura and D. pseudoobscura.
source: Interestingly, not all metrics related to sensory organs on the head were different between these closely related species. For example, the maxillary palps (Figure 1G) did not display any significant variation in surface area, but we do note differences in the ocelli (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements of maxillary palp surface area shown in Figure 1G.

claim: There are differences in the ocelli between D. subobscura and D. pseudoobscura.
source: Interestingly, not all metrics related to sensory organs on the head were different between these closely related species. For example, the maxillary palps (Figure 1G) did not display any significant variation in surface area, but we do note differences in the ocelli (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements of ocelli shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–E.

claim: Changes to sensory systems on the head appear mostly restricted to the antenna and to the visual sensory modalities in D. subobscura and D. pseudoobscura.
source: Thus, these changes to sensory systems on the head appear mostly restricted to the antenna and to the visual sensory modalities.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that maxillary palps did not differ significantly while eyes and antennae did.

claim: D. pseudoobscura has a relative increase of the antennal lobe size compared to D. subobscura after correcting for adult size.
source: After correcting for adult size (using the remaining hemisphere or central brain volume as a reference for each species; in grey) (Keesey et al., 2019), we identified a relative increase of the AL size for D. pseudoobscura (Figure 2C), as well as a relative decrease of the size of its OL (Figure 2D) when compared to the same neuropils for D. subobscura adults.
evidence: This claim is supported by volumetric measurements of brain neuropils shown in Figure 2C.

claim: D. pseudoobscura has a relative decrease of the size of its optic lobe compared to D. subobscura after correcting for adult size.
source: After correcting for adult size (using the remaining hemisphere or central brain volume as a reference for each species; in grey) (Keesey et al., 2019), we identified a relative increase of the AL size for D. pseudoobscura (Figure 2C), as well as a relative decrease of the size of its OL (Figure 2D) when compared to the same neuropils for D. subobscura adults.
evidence: This claim is supported by volumetric measurements of brain neuropils shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The inverse values between the antennal lobe and optic lobe correspond strongly to the variations measured in the external morphology of D. subobscura and D. pseudoobscura.
source: These inverse values between the two sensory systems correspond strongly to the variations we measured in the external morphology, where one species had larger eyes but smaller antennae, and vice versa.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the correlation between external morphology and brain neuropil measurements.

claim: All brain regions of the optic lobe are bigger in D. subobscura when corrected for total brain size, but only the medulla is significantly larger.
source: Moreover, to highlight the regions of the OL that show the largest increases, we provide similar metrics for relative size for the lobula plate, lobula and the medulla (Figure 2E), where all brain regions (again when corrected for total brain size; in grey) are bigger in D. subobscura, but only the medulla is significantly larger.
evidence: This claim is supported by volumetric measurements of optic lobe subregions shown in Figure 2E.

claim: D. subobscura displays light-dependent courtship and will not successfully copulate in the dark.
source: Previous research has shown that D. subobscura displays light-dependent courtship, and will not successfully copulate in the dark (Wallace and Dobzhansky, 1946; Grossfield, 1971; Spieth, 1952).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: D. pseudoobscura mating is light-independent, and courtship can successfully occur regardless of light conditions.
source: Counter to this, D. pseudoobscura mating is light-independent, and courtship can successfully occur regardless of light conditions (Brown, 1964; Wallace and Dobzhansky, 1946; Grossfield, 1971; Ripfel and Becker, 1982; Spassky, 1967).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: D. pseudoobscura males orient themselves either behind or to the side of the female during courtship.
source: D. pseudoobscura males oriented themselves either behind or to the side of the female during courtship, often forming a right angle to her with the male head focusing on the last few abdominal segments of the potential mate (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations from courtship videos and images shown in Figure 3A.

claim: D. pseudoobscura males perform characteristic wing vibrations and singing during courtship.
source: Next, this species performed characteristic wing vibrations and singing, with the outstretched wing always nearest to and in the direction of the head of the female (Figure 3A), and with the male constantly in pursuit of the female from behind or from the side.
evidence: This claim is supported by observations from courtship videos and images shown in Figure 3A.

claim: D. subobscura males often dart around in a circular arc to put themselves directly in front of the path of the female during courtship.
source: In stark contrast, observations of the courtship of D. subobscura showed that the males of this species often dart around in a circular arc to put themselves directly in front of the path of the female, and appear to arrest her movement (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations from courtship videos and images shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: Most of the courtship behaviors of D. subobscura males occur in front of the female and within her visual field.
source: This frontal positioning by the D. subobscura male results in most of the subsequent courtship behaviors occurring in front of the female and within her visual field, including the male wing displays.
evidence: This claim is inferred from observations of courtship behavior and positioning.

claim: D. subobscura males were not observed to vibrate the outstretched wing during courtship.
source: Here, D. subobscura was not observed to vibrate the outstretched wing (unlike D. pseudoobscura males, which are known to sing), and instead, seemed to angle or tilt the outstretched wing during the display, possibly as a flash of color via wing interference patterns (WIPs) (Shevtsova et al., 2011) or another visual exhibition for the female (Figure 3B,D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations from courtship videos.

claim: D. subobscura males angle or tilt the outstretched wing during courtship display, possibly as a flash of color via wing interference patterns or another visual exhibition for the female.
source: Here, D. subobscura was not observed to vibrate the outstretched wing (unlike D. pseudoobscura males, which are known to sing), and instead, seemed to angle or tilt the outstretched wing during the display, possibly as a flash of color via wing interference patterns (WIPs) (Shevtsova et al., 2011) or another visual exhibition for the female (Figure 3B,D,E).
evidence: This claim is based on observations from courtship videos and speculation about the function of the wing display.

claim: D. pseudoobscura significantly preferred to enter the Y-tube arm that was in shadow and darkened.
source: We observed that the smaller-eyed D. pseudoobscura significantly preferred to enter the Y-tube arm that was in shadow and darkened (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by phototaxis behavioral data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: D. subobscura significantly preferred the Y-tube arm that was in full light.
source: In contrast, the larger-eyed adult D. subobscura significantly preferred the Y-tube arm that was in full light.
evidence: This claim is supported by phototaxis behavioral data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Males of both D. pseudoobscura and D. subobscura showed a stronger trend of light preference than females, though this trend was not significant.
source: In both species, the males showed a stronger trend of light preference than females; however, this trend was not significant (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by phototaxis behavioral data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: There was a trend that D. pseudoobscura were slightly faster to make a choice in the Y-tube than D. subobscura.
source: We also noted no significant differences in the time it took flies to make a choice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), but there was a trend that D. pseudoobscura were slighty faster, as were the males of both species when compared to females.
evidence: This claim is supported by time measurements from phototaxis experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Males of both species were slightly faster to make a choice in the Y-tube than females.
source: We also noted no significant differences in the time it took flies to make a choice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), but there was a trend that D. pseudoobscura were slighty faster, as were the males of both species when compared to females.
evidence: This claim is supported by time measurements from phototaxis experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: There is a steady variance in positive or negative phototaxis across five obscura species examined.
source: Subsequently, we again repeated the same behavioral regimes using these new obscura members, including both y-tube phototaxis as well as species-specific courtship ethology. In these cases, we documented a rather steady variance in positive or negative phototaxis across this growing phylogenetic examination, with our initial two species (e.g. D. pseudoobscura and D. subobscura) representing the two extremes (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by phototaxis behavioral data across five species shown in Figure 5D.

claim: D. pseudoobscura and D. subobscura represent the two extremes of phototaxis behavior among the five obscura species examined.
source: Subsequently, we again repeated the same behavioral regimes using these new obscura members, including both y-tube phototaxis as well as species-specific courtship ethology. In these cases, we documented a rather steady variance in positive or negative phototaxis across this growing phylogenetic examination, with our initial two species (e.g. D. pseudoobscura and D. subobscura) representing the two extremes (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by phototaxis behavioral data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: There is a consistent change in male courtship behavior across obscura species, as measured by the percentage of time the male spends in front of the female during his display.
source: Similarly, we also observed a consistent change in male courtship behavior, as measured by the percentage of time the male of each new species spent in front of the female during his dance or mating display.
evidence: This claim is supported by courtship behavioral data across multiple species.

claim: Diameter of ommatidia does not vary between the five obscura species examined.
source: By documenting the relationship between our ommatidium counts and our estimates of the surface area of the compound eye, we conclude that diameter of ommatidia does not vary between our species (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), and we conclude that surface area is a consistently accurate metric for estimating the number of visual facets in the obscura group (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements of ommatidia diameter shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Surface area is a consistently accurate metric for estimating the number of visual facets in the obscura group.
source: By documenting the relationship between our ommatidium counts and our estimates of the surface area of the compound eye, we conclude that diameter of ommatidia does not vary between our species (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), and we conclude that surface area is a consistently accurate metric for estimating the number of visual facets in the obscura group (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the consistent relationship between eye surface area and ommatidia number shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Larger EF ratios correspond tightly with increases in positive phototaxis across obscura species.
source: Interestingly, we also describe correlations between EF ratio and phototaxis across our species, as well as the percentage of courtship the male spends in front of the female (Figure 5F,G). In both instances, larger EF ratios correspond tightly with increases in positive phototaxis (i.e. attraction to light) and correspond strongly with increases in courtship behaviors generated while in front of the female, which we presume are related to the importance of visual sensory signals.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Larger EF ratios correspond strongly with increases in courtship behaviors generated while in front of the female.
source: Interestingly, we also describe correlations between EF ratio and phototaxis across our species, as well as the percentage of courtship the male spends in front of the female (Figure 5F,G). In both instances, larger EF ratios correspond tightly with increases in positive phototaxis (i.e. attraction to light) and correspond strongly with increases in courtship behaviors generated while in front of the female, which we presume are related to the importance of visual sensory signals.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Courtship behaviors generated while in front of the female are related to the importance of visual sensory signals.
source: Interestingly, we also describe correlations between EF ratio and phototaxis across our species, as well as the percentage of courtship the male spends in front of the female (Figure 5F,G). In both instances, larger EF ratios correspond tightly with increases in positive phototaxis (i.e. attraction to light) and correspond strongly with increases in courtship behaviors generated while in front of the female, which we presume are related to the importance of visual sensory signals.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the presumption that frontal courtship behaviors are related to visual signals.

claim: Some of the largest behavioral differences occur between closest phylogenetic relatives, including D. pseudoobscura and D. persimilis.
source: Here we note that some of the largest behavioral differences (i.e. slope between individual species) still occur between closest phylogenetic relatives, including D. pseudoobscura and D. persimilis (Figure 5F,G), which represent the most-studied and well-published sympatric species pair from the obscura group.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5F,G.

claim: D. pseudoobscura and D. persimilis represent the most-studied and well-published sympatric species pair from the obscura group.
source: Here we note that some of the largest behavioral differences (i.e. slope between individual species) still occur between closest phylogenetic relatives, including D. pseudoobscura and D. persimilis (Figure 5F,G), which represent the most-studied and well-published sympatric species pair from the obscura group.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about these species.

claim: In sympatric species, larger behavioral variations occur than changes in morphology, suggesting that even small tradeoffs in olfactory or visual sensory systems can generate robust changes in behavior.
source: In these sympatric species, we see larger behavioral variations (y-axis) than changes in morphology (x-axis), suggesting that perhaps even small tradeoffs in olfactory or visual sensory systems can generate robust changes in behavior (Figure 5F,G).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of behavioral and morphological data shown in Figure 5F,G.

claim: Changes in phototaxis between sympatric species appear to be stronger and more acute than changes in courtship dynamics.
source: Here, we note that changes in phototaxis between sympatric species appear to be stronger and more acute than changes in courtship dynamics (Figure 5D,F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of behavioral data shown in Figure 5D,F,G.

claim: The slope of the correlation between phototaxis and EF Ratio for the sympatric species is greater than the slope related to the rest of the obscura subgroup.
source: Moreover, we observe that the slope of the correlation between phototaxis and EF Ratio for the sympatric species is greater than the slope related to the rest of the obscura subgroup (Figure 5F; orange vs grey).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Sources of light gradients may create strong selective pressures and isolation mechanisms that lead to speciation events or stabilizing selection for opposing phototaxis within otherwise overlapping habitats.
source: In this study, we hypothesize that sources of light gradients may also create strong selective pressures and isolation mechanisms that in turn lead to speciation events or stabilizing selection for opposing phototaxis within otherwise overlapping habitats, such as arboreal forests.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: Light gradients most likely work in tandem with inverse changes in pheromone or chemosensory changes to further provide avenues for species divergence.
source: Moreover, we propose that these light gradients most likely work in tandem with inverse changes in pheromone or chemosensory changes to further provide avenues for species divergence.
evidence: This is a proposal by the authors based on their findings and speculation.

claim: Arboreal forest microhabitats have been addressed previously as sources for spatial separation between species.
source: Arboreal forest microhabitats have been addressed previously as sources for spatial separation between species (Atkinson and Miller, 1980; Montgomery and Merrill, 2017; Penariol and Madi-Ravazzi, 2013; Taylor and Powell, 1978), including studies directly related to the field-sampling of members of the family Drosophilidae, often with the division of species occurring in proximity to the forest edge.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Sources of light may be one of the ambient forces driving the observed tradeoff in the evolution of eye and antenna size.
source: While the evolutionary selective pressures and their effects on the relative size of various components of the nervous system have not been previously examined, it has been suggested that sources of light may be one of the ambient forces driving the observed tradeoff in the evolution of these two sensory structures (Keesey et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Several monophyletic species within the obscura group deviate significantly in regards to both eye and antenna morphology.
source: Here we demonstrate that several monophyletic species within the obscura group, despite being close relatives, deviate significantly in regards to both eye and antenna morphology (Figure 1), as well as in their corresponding neuropils for vision and olfaction (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological measurements shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Variation in sensory systems positively correlates with both courtship behavior and environmental habitat preferences in obscura species.
source: In addition, we observe that this variation in sensory systems positively correlates with both courtship behavior (Figure 3) and environmental habitat preferences (Figure 4), especially as related to the relative importance of visual stimuli or sources of light, which appears to be of opposing value between these sibling species (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral and morphological data shown in Figures 3, 4, and 5.

claim: The relative importance of visual stimuli or sources of light appears to be of opposing value between D. pseudoobscura and D. subobscura.
source: In addition, we observe that this variation in sensory systems positively correlates with both courtship behavior (Figure 3) and environmental habitat preferences (Figure 4), especially as related to the relative importance of visual stimuli or sources of light, which appears to be of opposing value between these sibling species (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the opposing phototaxis behaviors and courtship strategies of the two species.

claim: A tradeoff or inverse resource allocation between vision and olfaction has been documented across more than 60 species within the Drosophila genus.
source: Previous work has documented this tradeoff or inverse resource allocation between vision and olfaction across more than 60 species within the Drosophila genus (Keesey IW et al., 2019), but the ecological mechanisms and selective pressures underlying this divergence have not been studied as explicitly in monophyletic species groups or subgroups.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: There has been documentation of a recent geographical overlap between D. pseudoobscura and D. subobscura in North America.
source: In addition, there has been documentation of a recent geographical overlap between D.pseudoobscura and D. subobscura in North America, which might make for an ideal field study in the future to test our hypotheses regarding environmental partitioning and the evolution of sensory variation (Noor, 1998; Pascual et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: D. pseudoobscura and D. persimilis have been well established as sympatric species.
source: However, the species D. pseudoobscura and D persimilis have been well established as sympatric (Crysnanto and Obbard, 2019; O'Grady, 1999), and already act as models for genetic variation in phototaxis and courtship (Brown, 1965; Brown, 1964; Hernández and Fabre, 2016; Noor and Aquadro, 1998; Ripfel and Becker, 1982).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: D. pseudoobscura and D. persimilis act as models for genetic variation in phototaxis and courtship.
source: However, the species D. pseudoobscura and D persimilis have been well established as sympatric (Crysnanto and Obbard, 2019; O'Grady, 1999), and already act as models for genetic variation in phototaxis and courtship (Brown, 1965; Brown, 1964; Hernández and Fabre, 2016; Noor and Aquadro, 1998; Ripfel and Becker, 1982).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Significant deviation in visual and olfactory behavior occurs in D. pseudoobscura and D. persimilis, including both phototactic response and potential visual bias during male courtship.
source: In these two evolutionarily sympatric species (i.e. D. pseudoobscura and D persimilis), we demonstrate significant deviation in visual and olfactory behavior, including both phototactic response and potential visual bias during male courtship (Figure 5D–G), thus supporting our initial proposal that variance in sensory investment occurs even within closest, sympatric species across this genus.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5D–G.

claim: Variance in sensory investment occurs even within closest, sympatric species across the Drosophila genus.
source: In these two evolutionarily sympatric species (i.e. D. pseudoobscura and D persimilis), we demonstrate significant deviation in visual and olfactory behavior, including both phototactic response and potential visual bias during male courtship (Figure 5D–G), thus supporting our initial proposal that variance in sensory investment occurs even within closest, sympatric species across this genus.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral and morphological data from sympatric species.

claim: Close insect relatives may divide host or habitat resources through niche partitioning by inversely prioritizing the relative importance of visual stimuli as compared to olfactory stimuli.
source: In the present study, we test the hypothesis that close insect relatives may divide host or habitat resources through niche partitioning by inversely prioritizing the relative importance of visual stimuli as compared to those stimuli that are olfactory.
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested in the study.

claim: Monophyletic species often possess inversely correlated eye and antenna sizes despite being close relatives and despite sharing seemingly identical hosts and environmental preferences.
source: This explanation would be consistent with previous observations that monophyletic species often possess inversely correlated eye and antenna sizes despite being close relatives and despite sharing seemingly identical hosts and environmental preferences (Gaspar et al., 2020; Keesey et al., 2019; Özer and Carle, 2020; Ramaekers et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The sensory inversion across the obscura group occurs across close, sympatric relatives, as well as across several populations or strains of each species.
source: In addition, this hypothesis continues to be consistent with the more in depth analyses afforded by the present study, which documents this sensory inversion across the obscura group, including across close, sympatric relatives, as well as across several populations or strains of each species (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data across multiple populations shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Microhabitats often arise in nature, as landscapes are inherently non-uniform.
source: Microhabitats often arise in nature, as landscapes are inherently non-uniform (Martin, 1998; Scheffers et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Plant hosts and other nutritional resources such as fungi and yeasts can differ greatly between forest edge and forest interior.
source: Moreover, that plant hosts and other nutritional resources such as fungi and yeasts can differ greatly between forest edge and forest interior (Bächli et al., 2006; Łuczaj and Sadowska, 1997; Penariol and Madi-Ravazzi, 2013; Toda, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Flora and fauna can vary in both their relative abundance as well as their innate preferences across microclimates within a single habitat.
source: Thus, it is well recognized that flora and fauna can vary in both their relative abundance as well as their innate preferences across microclimates within a single habitat, where the fitness of a Drosophila species is intimately tied to its ability to compete for resources within its own environmental niche (Koerte et al., 2020; Qiao et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The fitness of a Drosophila species is intimately tied to its ability to compete for resources within its own environmental niche.
source: Thus, it is well recognized that flora and fauna can vary in both their relative abundance as well as their innate preferences across microclimates within a single habitat, where the fitness of a Drosophila species is intimately tied to its ability to compete for resources within its own environmental niche (Koerte et al., 2020; Qiao et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Both D. pseudoobscura and D. subobscura share similar crepuscular activity.
source: Conversely, it has been well-documented that both D. pseudoobscura and D. subobscura share similar crepuscular activity (Atkinson and Miller, 1980; Bächli et al., 2006; Michell and Epling, 1951; Noor, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Circadian rhythms or seasonal activities of feeding or courtship do not play any distinct role in the observed evolutionary divergence in relative eye or antenna size between D. pseudoobscura and D. subobscura.
source: Thus, at this juncture we do not feel that the circadian rhythms or seasonal activities of feeding or courtship play any distinct role in the observed evolutionary divergence in relative eye or antenna size.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that both species share similar crepuscular activity.

claim: D. subobscura simply uses consistent visual stimuli as a species-defining trait, perhaps initiated via a preference for a better-lit arena to perform their courtship ritual and to attract a potential mate.
source: Thus, we suggest that it is more likely that D. subobscura simply uses consistent visual stimuli as a species-defining trait, perhaps initiated via a preference for a better-lit arena to perform their courtship ritual and to attract a potential mate.
evidence: This is a suggestion based on the observed courtship behavior and phototaxis.

claim: D. subobscura prefers microhabitats such as a forest edge or an open forest canopy where visual elements of courtship such as wing displays would be more optimally employed.
source: This would include such microhabitats as a forest edge or an open forest canopy (Figure 4C), where visual elements of courtship such as wing displays would be more optimally employed for species identification and female sexual selection given the increases in light availability.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed phototaxis and courtship behavior.

claim: D. pseudoobscura may be more likely to prefer darker, inner-forest habitats, while D. subobscura would prefer the forest edge or sections of open canopies within the same forest environment.
source: Here, we suggest while these species are assumed to be linked via a forest ecology (Bächli et al., 2006; Burla et al., 1986; Michell and Epling, 1951), that D. pseudoobscura may be more likely to prefer darker, inner-forest habitats, while D. subobscura would prefer the forest edge or sections of open canopies within the same forest environment (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a suggestion based on the observed phototaxis behavior and citations to previous research.

claim: Light preference would create opposing spatial regions of highest abundance, where each species would reduce overlap with the other by tuning their sensory systems towards either larger-eyes and positive phototaxis, or smaller eyes and negative phototaxis.
source: This light preference would therefore create opposing spatial regions of highest abundance, where each species would reduce overlap with the other by tuning their sensory systems towards either larger-eyes and positive phototaxis, or smaller eyes and negative phototaxis.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the observed sensory and behavioral differences.

claim: This shift in the nervous system would affect both courtship and host preference.
source: We thus propose that this shift in the nervous system would then affect both courtship and host preference.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the observed correlations between sensory investment and behavior.

claim: Field studies in the 1980s using baited traps did not find a distinct difference in capture across light versus dark areas for D. subobscura.
source: Here, field studies in the 1980s using baited traps did not find a distinct difference in capture across light versus dark areas for D. subobscura (Atkinson and Miller, 1980).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Of the 1200-1500 species of Drosophila that have been documented, none have been described to be nocturnal.
source: It is important to note that, to our knowledge, of the 1200–1500 species of Drosophila that have been documented, none have been described to be nocturnal (which could be an alternative factor for the evolution of especially large and light-sensitive eyes).
evidence: This is stated as knowledge based on the authors' understanding of the literature.

claim: Increases in eye size for the Drosophila genus correlate strongly with positive phototaxis and correlate with visually mediated courtship.
source: Thus, it is reasonable that increases in eye size for this genus correlate so strongly with positive phototaxis and correlate with visually mediated courtship (Figure 5F,G), and we propose this occurrence may extend toward all members of the Drosophila genus (Keesey et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation data shown in Figure 5F,G and a citation to previous work.

claim: The importance of potential visual displays in courtship and predator avoidance has been previously examined in some Lepidopterans.
source: Moreover, the importance of potential visual displays in courtship and predator avoidance has also been previously examined in some Lepidopterans, including phylogenetic studies across spatial and ecological gradients (Montgomery and Merrill, 2017), as well as in regards to the genetics of wing pigmentation, especially wing spots (Zhang and Reed, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The utilization of forest openings are well studied in avian biology, where males often construct and clear elaborate arenas to perform intricate visual displays for females.
source: The utilization of forest openings are well studied in avian biology, where males often construct and clear elaborate arenas to perform intricate visual displays for females (i.e. the genus Parotia or six-plumed birds of paradise) (Ligon et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: It remains unclear which of phototaxis or visual courtship occurs first, and which behavior subsequently drives a correlation in the other trait over the course of evolutionary time.
source: Here we demonstrate that tendency among these five obscura species, although it remains unclear which of these behavioral phenotypes occurs first (e.g. phototaxis or visual courtship), and which behavior subsequently drives a correlation in the other trait over the course of evolutionary time.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of uncertainty about the evolutionary sequence of events.

claim: Minor shifts in morphology and neurobiology between sensory components of the nervous system first create exaggerated changes in phototaxis behavior, perhaps due to a spontaneous developmental mutation.
source: Thus, we hypothesize minor shifts in morphology and neurobiology between sensory components of the nervous system first create exaggerated changes in phototaxis behavior, perhaps due to a spontaneous developmental mutation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: Initial changes in phototaxis might initially separate species spatially and then subsequently, courtship characteristics start to drift apart, which ultimately leads to a division that no longer allows successful mating or progeny to occur.
source: This might initially separate species spatially and then subsequently, courtship characteristics start to drift apart (e.g. chemical, auditory or visual cues), which ultimately leads to a division that no longer allows successful mating or progeny to occur and thus that incipient species diverge more permanently.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors about the sequence of speciation events.

claim: The visual system is inherently expensive to maintain.
source: As the visual system is inherently expensive to maintain (Niven and Laughlin, 2008), this could produce a reduction in the visual system, with the evolutionary pressure being energy preservation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Reduction in visual investment could be a consequence, not a driving force, of niche partitioning.
source: As the visual system is inherently expensive to maintain (Niven and Laughlin, 2008), this could produce a reduction in the visual system, with the evolutionary pressure being energy preservation. Thus, reduction in visual investment would be a consequence, not a driving force, of niche partitioning.
evidence: This is an alternative hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Zero Drosophila species are described as nocturnal.
source: Again, we also point out that zero Drosophila species are described as nocturnal, thus variation in eye size may be under significantly different pressures than nocturnal insects, such as crickets (i.e. Orthopterans), which have often greatly increased their visual investment for their nocturnal activity.
evidence: This is stated as knowledge based on the authors' understanding of the literature.

claim: The more significant changes in phototaxis occur between close, genetic relatives, which appear prior to significant changes in courtship.
source: Here in the present study, we observe that the more significant changes in phototaxis still occur between close, genetic relatives, which appear prior to significant changes in courtship (Figure 5D,F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5D,F,G.

claim: Niche partitioning, character displacement, and response to light gradients are the stronger initial driving forces of the evolution and speciation within the obscura group.
source: As such, we continue to predict that niche partitioning, character displacement, and response to light gradients are the stronger initial driving forces of the evolution and speciation within the obscura group, where the novel environmental conditions drive sensory investment that in turn optimizes the courtship success of each species in this new niche.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the authors' findings and interpretation.

claim: Novel environmental conditions drive sensory investment that in turn optimizes the courtship success of each species in this new niche.
source: As such, we continue to predict that niche partitioning, character displacement, and response to light gradients are the stronger initial driving forces of the evolution and speciation within the obscura group, where the novel environmental conditions drive sensory investment that in turn optimizes the courtship success of each species in this new niche.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the authors' findings and interpretation.

claim: Male D. subobscura do not sing, and thus do not vibrate their wings during display.
source: Moreover, it has been shown that male D. subobscura do not sing, and thus do not vibrate their wings during display, but we do observe midleg tapping or drumming, which may instead be the auditory component of their courtship ethology.
evidence: This claim is stated as established knowledge and supported by observations in the study.

claim: Midleg tapping or drumming may be the auditory component of D. subobscura courtship ethology.
source: Moreover, it has been shown that male D. subobscura do not sing, and thus do not vibrate their wings during display, but we do observe midleg tapping or drumming, which may instead be the auditory component of their courtship ethology.
evidence: This is a speculation based on observations of courtship behavior.

claim: Previous research has shown an expansion of the fruitless positive labeled cells in the optic lobes of D. subobscura as compared to D. melanogaster.
source: However, previous research has already shown an expansion of the fruitless positive labeled cells in the optic lobes of D. subobscura as compared to D. melanogaster (Tanaka et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The expansion of fruitless positive labeled cells in the optic lobes is indicative of an evolutionary investment in visual modalities for courtship success.
source: Thus, while this pathway has not been addressed yet in D. pseudoobscura or any other members of the obscura group, it is perhaps again indicative of an evolutionary investment in visual modalities for courtship success, given the visual connection to this fruitless labeled neural pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on the citation to previous research and the known function of the fruitless pathway.

claim: Variation in visual and olfactory sensory system development occurs for more than just mating purposes, and appears to match ecological deviations in behavioral phototaxis and microhabitat preferences for light within a shared ecological niche.
source: Nevertheless, it is apparent from our current data that variation in visual and olfactory sensory system development occurs for more than just mating purposes, and appears to match ecological deviations in behavioral phototaxis and microhabitat preferences for light within a shared ecological niche.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined behavioral and morphological data presented in the study.

claim: D. subobscura males have significantly longer trichoid sensilla than D. pseudoobscura males.
source: Here, we note a difference in trichoid length between males of the two obscura species, with D. subobscura having significantly longer sensillum than D. pseudoobscura.
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: D. subobscura consistently had larger ocelli than D. pseudoobscura.
source: Average ocelli length from males and females of each species, where D. subobscura consistently had larger ocelli.
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–D.

claim: There was no significant difference in ommatidium diameter between D. subobscura and D. pseudoobscura.
source: Average ommatidium diameters, where there was no significant difference between our two obscura species.
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F.

claim: There were no significant differences in ommatidia diameter across the five obscura species examined.
source: Repeated measures of ommatidia diameter were generated and statistically compared between our five obscura species, though we did not document any significant differences in diameter.
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: All brain regions of the optic lobe (lobula plate, lobula, and medulla) are bigger in D. subobscura when corrected for total brain size.
source: Moreover, to highlight the regions of the OL that show the largest increases, we provide similar metrics for relative size for the lobula plate, lobula and the medulla (Figure 2E), where all brain regions (again when corrected for total brain size; in grey) are bigger in D. subobscura, but only the medulla is significantly larger.
evidence: This claim is supported by volumetric measurements shown in Figure 2E.

claim: D. subobscura males spend significantly more time in front of the female during courtship compared to D. pseudoobscura males.
source: Time that males spent within the female visual field during courtship.
evidence: This claim is supported by courtship behavioral data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Stable structural wing interference patterns are observed across the otherwise clear wings of males of both D. pseudoobscura and D. subobscura.
source: Stable structural wing interference patterns observed across the otherwise clear wings of males of both species.
evidence: This claim is supported by images of wing interference patterns shown in Figure 3E.

claim: 84% of D. pseudoobscura males chose the dark arm of the Y-tube.
source: Percentages of male and female flies of both species choosing the well-lit or darkened arm of the y-tube.
evidence: This claim is supported by phototaxis behavioral data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 76% of D. subobscura males chose the light arm of the Y-tube.
source: Percentages of male and female flies of both species choosing the well-lit or darkened arm of the y-tube.
evidence: This claim is supported by phototaxis behavioral data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: These obscura species, despite sharing a forest ecology, create a reduction in either host resource or mating competition via their different preferences toward edge and open canopy environmental conditions, as related directly to their innate preferences for light intensity.
source: Here we propose that these obscura species, despite sharing a forest ecology, create a reduction in either host resource or mating competition via their different preferences toward edge and open canopy environmental conditions, as related directly to their innate preferences for light intensity.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the observed phototaxis behavior and ecological considerations.

claim: Eye-to-funiculus ratio (EF ratio) varies significantly between the five obscura species examined.
source: Statistical assessments of average EF Ratio between each species.
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Eye surface area is positively correlated with the number of ommatidia across the five obscura species examined.
source: Morphological measurements of eye surface area and the number of ommatidia collected from lateral views of each species.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: There is a positive correlation between EF ratio and positive phototaxis across all tested obscura species.
source: Correlation between EF ratio and positive phototaxis for all tested obscura species.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: There is a positive correlation between EF ratio and the percentage of male courtship spent in front of the female across obscura species.
source: Correlation between EF ratio and the percentage of male courtship spent in front of the female during his dance or display ethology.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Courtship initiation and success was observed to be highest between 18-24 degrees Celsius for both D. pseudoobscura and D. subobscura.
source: Here we optimized the temperature for both obscura species, where courtship initiation and success was observed to be highest between 18–24 degrees Celsius, which was a substantially lower temperature than previous examinations of D. melanogaster courtship.
evidence: This claim is based on observations during courtship experiments.

claim: The optimal courtship temperature for D. pseudoobscura and D. subobscura is substantially lower than that for D. melanogaster.
source: Here we optimized the temperature for both obscura species, where courtship initiation and success was observed to be highest between 18–24 degrees Celsius, which was a substantially lower temperature than previous examinations of D. melanogaster courtship.
evidence: This claim is based on observations during courtship experiments and comparison to previous research.

claim: Eight to ten females of each species were photographed for morphological measurements.
source: Eight to 10 females of these species were photographed using a Zeiss AXIO microscope, including lateral, dorsal, and frontal views.
evidence: This is a description of the methods used in the study.

claim: The antennal lobe size is relatively larger in D. pseudoobscura compared to D. subobscura after correcting for brain size.
source: After correcting for adult size (using the remaining hemisphere or central brain volume as a reference for each species; in grey) (Keesey et al., 2019), we identified a relative increase of the AL size for D. pseudoobscura (Figure 2C)
evidence: This claim is supported by volumetric measurements shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The optic lobe size is relatively smaller in D. pseudoobscura compared to D. subobscura after correcting for brain size.
source: After correcting for adult size (using the remaining hemisphere or central brain volume as a reference for each species; in grey) (Keesey et al., 2019), we identified a relative increase of the AL size for D. pseudoobscura (Figure 2C), as well as a relative decrease of the size of its OL (Figure 2D) when compared to the same neuropils for D. subobscura adults.
evidence: This claim is supported by volumetric measurements shown in Figure 2D.
